title: People who frequently use ChatGPT for writing tasks are accurate and robust detectors of AI-generated text (Russell, Karpinska, Iyyer; ACL 2025)
claim: Annotators who often use LLMs for writing detect AI articles near-perfectly; non-expert annotators are at chance yet confident. Experts cited vocabulary most.
result: 300 non-fiction articles <1000 words (GPT-4o, Claude-3.5-Sonnet, o1-Pro). Expert 5-vote majority TPR 99.3 / FPR 0 (one article missed). Individual experts TPR 59.3-97.3, FPR 1.3-12. Nonexperts avg TPR 56.7 / FPR 51.7, confidence 4.03. Clues cited (share of explanations): vocabulary 53.1% ('crucial','testament'), sentence structure 35.9%, grammar/punctuation 24.8% (AI flawless, humans have small errors), originality 23.7% (AI safe/predictable), quotes 22.3% (overly formal/uniform), clarity 19.5%. Humanized o1-Pro: expert majority 100/0. Summarizer noted the paper has internal number inconsistencies (FPR 4.0 vs 3.3).
implication: Frequent LLM users are the only human instrument that worked; recruit them, not generic readers. Articles were long and non-fiction: short UI/game lines were not tested, so a human check on one line is weaker than on 300 words; use several experts and majority vote. The clue list (vocabulary, flawless grammar, safe/predictable, over-formal) is a usable rubric.

title: Same paper: automatic detectors vs experts
claim: Detector ranking on the same 300 articles; Pangram and GPTZero strong, Binoculars/Fast-DetectGPT/RADAR weak, prompted GPT-4o weak.
result: TPR/FPR: Pangram 98.0/2; Pangram Humanizers 99.3/2.7; GPTZero 85.3/0.7; Fast-DetectGPT 80.0/7.2; Binoculars (accuracy threshold) 66.7/1.3, (low-FPR) 40.0/0; RADAR 15.3/2; best GPT-4o prompt-based detector (CoT+guidebook) 78.0/10.7. Humanized o1-Pro: Pangram 90.0/6.7, GPTZero 46.7/3.3, Fast-DetectGPT 23.3/3.3, Binoculars 6.67/0. Paraphrased GPT-4o: Pangram 100/0, GPTZero 100/0, Fast-DetectGPT 56.7/3.3.
implication: Perplexity-family detectors (Binoculars, Fast-DetectGPT) are poor on modern models and humanized text; do not use for checking rewrites. A prompted LLM as detector got 10.7% FPR at best, i.e. an LLM asked 'is this AI?' is a noisy flagger even on long text. Paper does not analyze short texts.

title: GPT detectors are biased against non-native English writers (Liang et al.)
claim: Perplexity-based detectors flag non-native (TOEFL) writing as AI; low-perplexity plain text is the false-positive trap.
result: 7 detectors, 91 TOEFL essays: avg FPR 61.22%; 18/91 (19.78%) flagged by all seven; 89/91 (97.80%) flagged by at least one. US 8th-grade essays near-perfect. GPT-4 vocabulary enrichment of TOEFL essays cut FPR 61.22% -> 11.77%; simplifying native essays raised misclassification.
implication: Plain, simple, low-perplexity human writing (and game/UI lines are short and plain) is exactly what older detectors call AI. A detector that has not been shown to pass known-human plain lines is not usable here. Study is 2023 and covers older detectors.

title: Technical Report on the Pangram AI-Generated Text Classifier
read: snippet (PDF unreadable by fetcher; figures via search summary)
claim: Vendor self-report: near-zero FPR including on non-native English corpora; edited text still slips.
result: Per search summary: FPR 0% on 91 TOEFL essays (held out from training), 0 FP on 3,907 ELLIPSE essays, 0.09% on 5,600 ICNALE; GPTZero 7.7% on TOEFL in the same report. When consumer AI 'substantially modified' human essays, Pangram labelled the result human 41% of the time. Not verified against the paper text.
implication: Vendor evidence, not independent. Treat the non-native FPR claim as unverified for short plain lines; run own known-human control.

title: Third party Pangram evals (vendor summary of Chicago Booth / UMD / VUB)
claim: Vendor page summarizing independent evaluations; Chicago Booth (Jabarian and Imas, BFI WP 2025-116 / NBER w34223) found Pangram lowest error; vendor page says Pangram returns no prediction for texts under 50 words, which conflicts with the working paper abstract saying it 'largely holds up' under 50 words.
result: Chicago Booth avg over 6 genres x 4 LLMs, FPR/FNR: Pangram 0.001/0.01; Originality 0.002/0.035; GPTZero 0.007/0.06; RoBERTa open-source FPR 0.50. Humanizer (StealthGPT): Pangram near 100% detection, GPTZero FNR 0.50+, Originality FNR up to 0.21 on short texts. VUB June 2026 peer-reviewed: Pangram 97.5% on fully AI text, 95% hybrid, 95% humanized, 0% FP on human text; GPTZero 0% on fully AI text in that setup (odd; vendor-reported).
implication: Source is Pangram marketing; the short-text claim is contradictory across sources. Test Pangram on actual 1-2 sentence lines before believing it, and check whether it refuses or returns a score.

title: Artificial Writing and Automated Detection (Jabarian, Imas; NBER w34223 / BFI 2025-116)
read: snippet (abstract via search; PDF unreadable by fetcher)
claim: Commercial detectors beat the open-source RoBERTa; Pangram the only one meeting FPR <= 0.005 cap without losing accuracy; Pangram performance 'largely holds up' on passages under 50 words and against humanizers, others case-dependent.
result: As stated in abstract summary: Pangram near-zero FPR and FNR on test set; policy cap FPR <= 0.005. GPTZero disputed it (said wrong API field was used) and reports vendor re-run: GPTZero 99.5% accuracy, Pangram 99.1%, Originality 85.0% (vendor-run, contested).
implication: Best independent evidence that a detector might work below 50 words, but dataset (reviews, blogs, news, novel excerpts, resumes) is not game lines, and vendors dispute each other. Pre-register the control: known-human short lines must score human.

title: Limits of LLM Text Detectors in Education (Gehring, Paassen)
claim: All four tested detectors degrade as text shortens; at under 50 words performance 'remains very limited'.
result: Ghostbuster 'considerable degradation below 250 words'; DetectGPT/Fast-DetectGPT decline for shorter inputs; RoBERTa smallest relative drop and best under 50 words but still very limited. Exact values only in a figure, not retrieved.
implication: Open-source/academic detectors are not reliable on one or two sentences. Do not use Binoculars-style scores for short lines.

title: Spotting LLMs With Binoculars (Hans et al., ICML 2024)
claim: Zero-shot detector claims >90% detection at 0.01% FPR on long documents; no short-text figure found.
result: Headline: over 90% of generated samples at 0.01% FPR (paper's document lengths). In Russell et al. on 300 modern-LLM articles Binoculars got only TPR 66.7 / FPR 1.3 (or 40.0 / 0 at the low-FPR threshold). Memorized/low-perplexity text causes false positives (per review).
implication: Paper headline numbers did not replicate on newer models in Russell et al.; skip for short lines.

title: LLM Evaluators Recognize and Favor Their Own Generations (Panickssery, Bowman, Feng; NeurIPS 2024)
claim: Judges recognize their own text above chance and prefer it; self-preference rises roughly linearly with self-recognition after fine-tuning. Zero-shot recognition is weak outside GPT-4.
result: News summarization (XSUM, CNN/DM). Zero-shot pairwise self-recognition confidence: GPT-4 0.672 (XSUM) / 0.747 (CNN); Llama-2-7b 0.514 / 0.505. Individual (single text) setting: GPT-4 0.5 on own text, unwilling to claim a text as its own. Human text is the easiest to separate from LLM text (GPT-4 confidence 0.71 on human text), so recognition partly reflects human-vs-LLM style. Fine-tuning on 500 examples gave >90% self-recognition (secondary summary).
implication: A judge model grading its own family's rewrite will favor it; use a different family than the one that wrote the line. Judging a single line in isolation (the individual setting) was near chance; pairwise human-vs-model is where models do best, so a known-human control in a pair is the right probe design.

title: Self-Preference Bias in LLM-as-a-Judge (Wataoka et al.)
claim: Self-preference is driven by familiarity: judges give higher scores to lower-perplexity text, whoever wrote it.
result: GPT-4 shows significant self-preference by the paper's metric; LLMs score lower-perplexity outputs higher than human evaluators do, regardless of generator. No numbers in the abstract.
implication: Smooth, predictable prose wins with every model judge, including text a human would call machine-like; model judges reward the thing we are trying to remove. Treat their preference as a signal of fluency, not of human-ness.

title: Self-Preference Bias in Rubric-Based Evaluation of Large Language Models (Pombal, Rei, Martins)
claim: Rubrics with binary per-criterion verdicts do not remove self-preference; multiple judges reduce but do not eliminate it.
result: Judges up to >50% more likely to wrongly mark a failed rubric item satisfied when the output is their own (objective benchmarks IFEval, LiveCodeBench); score shifts up to 10 points on HealthBench; negative rubrics and subjective topics worst.
implication: A rubric is not a defence against family bias. Use judges from other families than the writer and aggregate across them; rubric items framed as 'does it contain X' are riskier when negative.

title: Everyone prefers human writers, including AI
claim: Blind, humans and 13 LLM judges were about indifferent between human and AI passages; when labelled, both prefer 'human-written', and LLMs show the effect about 2.5x as strongly.
result: 30 Queneau Exercises in Style passages vs GPT-4 versions; 556 humans + 13 AI judges. Chose AI passage: humans 55.3% blind / 47.8% labelled / 61.5% counterfactual labels; AI judges 49.4% / 29.8% / 64.1%. Attribution bias humans +13.7 pp, AI +34.3 pp. Cross-model 14x14 study: 54.5% / 39.9% / 65.7%, bias +25.8 pp. All 13 judges positive bias (h 0.40 to 1.50).
implication: Never tell a judge which line is the model's or the human's; blind and shuffled. Blind judging showed no strong preference either way, so it is not evidence that LLM judges inflate AI prose here; the labelled bias is the bigger hazard.

title: Judging LLM-as-a-Judge with MT-Bench and Chatbot Arena (Zheng et al.)
claim: Position, verbosity and self-enhancement bias exist; GPT-4 agrees with humans >80%; swapping order is the standard control.
result: Position consistency after order swap (default prompt): GPT-4 65.0% (30.0% favored first, 5.0% second), GPT-3.5 46.2%, Claude-v1 23.8%. GPT-3.5 and Claude-v1 fell for a padded, longer answer; GPT-4 better. Self-enhancement noted for some models (numbers not retrieved).
implication: Run every pair in both orders and count only order-stable verdicts; lines in a UI are short so verbosity bias matters less, but length-matched pairs still needed.

title: Stylometric comparisons of human versus AI-generated creative writing (O'Sullivan, HSSC 2025) via search
claim: Burrows' Delta clusters short stories by generator model; occasional overlap of GPT-3.5 with humans.
result: GPT-3.5, GPT-4, Llama 70b stories cluster tightly by model; LLM text is stylistically more uniform than human.
implication: Models have distinct house styles, so a cross-family flagger may spot a different family's tics; but no study found where an LLM judge identifies another family's style. Evidence gap.

title: Null: cross-family LLM detecting or critiquing another family's style
claim: No controlled study found of Gemini/GPT flagging Claude prose, or vice versa. Blog guidance (practitioner, unsourced) recommends a different-family judge or a multi-family panel and stripping authorship cues.
result: Searches returned only self-preference papers and practitioner blogs; a null of searches, not proof of absence.
implication: The plan to use other families as flaggers rests on inference from self-preference and from Russell et al. (prompted GPT-4o as detector: FPR 10.7% at best, TPR 78%). It must be validated by the planned known-human control before trust.
